headings.title: Introduction and Clinical Objectives
headings.content: A high-calorie diet provides more energy than a standard maintenance diet, typically exceeding standard daily caloric requirements to promote weight gain, tissue repair, and positive nitrogen balance. Clinical objectives focus on reversing malnutrition, supporting hypermetabolic states such as severe burns or sepsis, and preventing severe muscle wasting in chronic illnesses.

headings.title: Nutritional Requirements and Macronutrient Distribution
headings.content:
Meeting increased energy needs requires careful balance among macronutrients:
- **Carbohydrates**: Serve as the primary, easily accessible source of energy, sparing protein for tissue synthesis.
- **Proteins**: Essential for cellular repair, immune function, and building lean muscle mass, often prescribed at higher grams per kilogram ratios.
- **Fats**: Offer the most concentrated form of energy, providing nine calories per gram to help boost total intake without requiring unmanageably large food volumes.

headings.title: Energy-Dense Food Sources
headings.content: When patients struggle to eat large quantities of food, selecting energy-dense items becomes essential. Nutrient-dense fats like groundnut paste, avocado, and vegetable oils add calories quickly without adding excessive bulk. Whole milk, eggs, beans, and locally available protein sources should be incorporated into meals and porridges to maximize caloric yield per bite.

headings.title: Nutritional Assessment and Monitoring
headings.content: Regular evaluation ensures the high-calorie regimen is effective and safe. Nurses track weekly weight trends, monitor intake and output charts, and observe for signs of digestive intolerance such as bloating or diarrhea. Laboratory markers, including serum albumin and electrolyte levels, help gauge metabolic response.

headings.title: Practical Meal Planning Strategies
headings.content: Successfully delivering extra calories requires creative meal planning tailored to local dietary habits. Instead of three large meals, patients often tolerate five to six small, frequent feedings better. Fortifying everyday foods by stirring in milk powder, butter, or oils increases energy intake effortlessly.

headings.title: Complications and Nursing Management
headings.content: Rapidly increasing caloric intake carries specific risks. Refeeding syndrome can occur in severely malnourished patients when carbohydrates trigger a sudden shift in electrolytes, leading to dangerous hypophosphatemia. Nurses must monitor electrolyte panels closely, introduce calories gradually, and watch for gastrointestinal distress like cramping or osmotic diarrhea.
